# Introduction

In this project we will explore the Bible, specifically King James Bible, in terms of data analysis.
The main goal is to train a model, that would take an arbitrary verse from the King James Bible and classify it into either Old or New Testament.
But before we get to the modeling part, we will first explore the data itself and see if there are any interesting patterns or insights that we can find.

# Data

The King James Bible dataset contains full text of the Bible divided into verses.
The dataset have been provided by our teachers[1] in a simple text format with non-standard delimiters.
The format (columns) of the dataset is the following: `Book Chapter:Verse    Text`, where:

:::{.column-margin}
\[1\]: [https://www.ksi.mff.cuni.cz/~holubova/NDBI048/](https://www.ksi.mff.cuni.cz/~holubova/NDBI048/https://www.ksi.mff.cuni.cz/~holubova/NDBI048/)
:::

- Book - name of the book where the verse can be found
- Chapter - chapter number
- Verse - verse number
- Text - text of the verse

Thus, after loading and parsing the data we have the following dataframe structure:

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

bible_df = pd.read_csv(
    "../data/bible.txt",
    sep="\t",
    header=None,
    names=["ref", "text"],
    engine="python",
)
parts = bible_df["ref"].str.extract(
    r"^(?P<book>.+?)\s+(?P<chapter>\d+):(?P<verse>\d+)$"
)

bible_df = pd.concat([parts, bible_df["text"]], axis=1)
bible_df.head()
```

As we can see, we have nicely prepared dataframe.
Another thing we can observe is that the text of the verses contains punctuation and is in mixed case.
We will deal with this later during the text preprocessing step.

## Data Quality Check

In this section we will perform a simple data quality check to ensure that our dataset is complete and does not contain any duplicates or missing values.
Firstly, let's look at some basic statistics of the dataset:

```{python}
print(f"Total number of lines (verses): {len(bible_df)}")
print(f"Number of duplicate lines: {bible_df.duplicated().sum()}")
print(f"Number of unique books: {bible_df['book'].nunique()}")
print(f"Number of chapters: {bible_df.groupby(['book', 'chapter']).ngroups}")
```

As we can see, there are no duplicate lines in the dataset.
On web \[[2](https://kingjamesbibledictionary.com/BibleFacts)\]\[[3](https://blackletterkingjamesbible.com/Library/BibleStatistics)\] we managed to find the following statistics about the King James Bible:

:::{.column-margin}
\[2\]: [https://kingjamesbibledictionary.com/BibleFacts](https://kingjamesbibledictionary.com/BibleFacts)

\[3\]: [https://blackletterkingjamesbible.com/Library/BibleStatistics](https://blackletterkingjamesbible.com/Library/BibleStatistics)
:::

- 66 books,
- 1,189 chapters,
- 31,102 verses.

These numbers match exactly with numbers obtained from our dataset.
Next, let's check for missing values:

```{python}
print(f"Number of missing values:\n{bible_df.isna().sum()}")
```

Luckily, there are no missing values in the dataset.
Thus, we can conclude that our dataset is complete and ready for further analysis.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

In this section we will perform some exploratory data analysis (EDA) to understand the structure and distribution of the data.
Firstly, we are going to look at the distribution of verses, then we will do a word based analysis of the text (of Bible as whole and later per Testament).
Finally we will compare the two Testaments based on the statistics we obtain.

As we can see from the histogram above, some books have significantly more verses than others.
For example, Psalms has the highest number of verses, while books like Obadiah and Philemon have very few verses.

Another thing that can be observed is that first half of the dataset (that should also correspond to Old Testament) has generally more verses per book compared to the second half (New Testament).

## Analysis per Testament

Here we will look at some basic statistics and visualizations for the New and Old Testament.
We will look again at number of verses, chapters and book, but additionally look also at the text itself.
For completeness we also include the statistics of the the whole Bible.
To maintain consistency we hence also include all the statistics for the whole Bible even though some of them are repeated from the previous sections.

Since we will be doing some Testament based text analysis, we need to do some preprocessing first.
Let's add a new column with indication of Testament and clean the text for word-based analysis.
This includes removing punctuation and converting everything to lowercase.

```{python}
def assign_testament(book):
    old_testament_books = [
        # Historical books
        "Genesis", "Exodus", "Leviticus", "Numbers", "Deuteronomy", "Joshua", "Judges", "Ruth", "1 Samuel", "2 Samuel", "1 Kings", "2 Kings", "1 Chronicles", "2 Chronicles", "Ezra", "Nehemiah", "Esther",
        # Poetic books
        "Job", "Psalms", "Proverbs", "Ecclesiastes", "Song of Solomon",
        # Prophetic books
        "Isaiah", "Jeremiah", "Lamentations", "Ezekiel", "Daniel", "Hosea", "Joel", "Amos", "Obadiah", "Jonah", "Micah", "Nahum", "Habakkuk", "Zephaniah", "Haggai", "Zechariah", "Malachi"
    ]

    new_testament_books = [
        # Gospels:
        "Matthew", "Mark", "Luke", "John",
        # Historical:
        "Acts",
        # Epistles:
        "Romans", "1 Corinthians", "2 Corinthians", "Galatians", "Ephesians", "Philippians", "Colossians", "1 Thessalonians", "2 Thessalonians", "1 Timothy", "2 Timothy", "Titus", "Philemon", "Hebrews", "James", "1 Peter", "2 Peter", "1 John", "2 John", "3 John", "Jude",
        # The Revelation:
        "Revelation"
    ]

    if book in old_testament_books:
        return "Old Testament"
    elif book in new_testament_books:
        return "New Testament"
    else:
        return "Unknown"

bible_df["testament"] = bible_df["book"].apply(assign_testament)

import re

def clean_text(text):
    text = text.lower()
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z\s]", " ", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    return text

bible_df["cleaned_text"] = bible_df["text"].apply(clean_text)
bible_df.head()
```

The way Testament is assigned also adds possibility to check if there are any unknown books in the dataset.
From the previous check we know that the number of books is correct, but we haven't checked if all the books really are books from the Bible.

```{python}
print(f"Unknown testaments present: {(bible_df['testament'] == 'Unknown').sum()}")
```

No verse is assigned to "Unknown" testament, thus we can be sure that all books in the dataset are indeed from the Bible.

Now we can proceed with the analysis of the Testaments.

## Bible
```{python}
with open("../data/stopwords-big.txt", "r") as f:
    stopwords = set(f.read().splitlines())

def basic_verses_chapters_books_stats(df, testament_name):
    print(f"Number of verses in {testament_name}: {len(df)}")
    print(f"Number of books in {testament_name}: {df['book'].nunique()}")
    print(f"Number of chapters in {testament_name}: {df.groupby(['book', 'chapter']).ngroups}")

def longest_shortest_books(df, testament_name):
    book_lengths = df.groupby('book').size()
    print(f"Longest book in {testament_name}: {book_lengths.idxmax()} ({book_lengths.max()} verses)")
    print(f"Shortest book in {testament_name}: {book_lengths.idxmin()} ({book_lengths.min()} verses)")

def longest_shortest_books_by_words(df, testament_name, stopwords = []):
    new_df = df.copy()
    new_df['word_count'] = new_df['cleaned_text'].apply(lambda x: len([word for word in x.split() if word not in stopwords]))
    book_word_lengths = new_df.groupby('book')['word_count'].sum()
    print(f"Longest book by words in {testament_name}: {book_word_lengths.idxmax()} ({book_word_lengths.max()} words)")
    print(f"Shortest book by words in {testament_name}: {book_word_lengths.idxmin()} ({book_word_lengths.min()} words)")

def average_verses_per_book(df, testament_name):
    book_lengths = df.groupby('book').size()
    average_verses = book_lengths.mean()
    print(f"Average number of verses per book in {testament_name}: {average_verses:.2f}")

def longest_shortest_verses(df, testament_name, stopwords = []):
    new_df = df.copy()
    new_df['word_count'] = new_df['cleaned_text'].apply(lambda x: len([word for word in x.split() if word not in stopwords]))
    longest_verse = new_df.loc[new_df['word_count'].idxmax()]
    shortest_verse = new_df.loc[new_df['word_count'].idxmin()]
    print(f"Longest verse in {testament_name}: {longest_verse['book']} {longest_verse['chapter']}:{longest_verse['verse']} ({longest_verse['word_count']} words)")
    print(f"Shortest verse in {testament_name}: {shortest_verse['book']} {shortest_verse['chapter']}:{shortest_verse['verse']} ({shortest_verse['word_count']} words)")

def average_words_per_verse(df, testament_name, stopwords = []):
    new_df = df.copy()
    new_df['word_count'] = new_df['cleaned_text'].apply(lambda x: len([word for word in x.split() if word not in stopwords]))
    average_words = new_df['word_count'].mean()
    print(f"Average number of words per verse in {testament_name}: {average_words:.2f}")

def plot_top_words(df, testament_name, number_of_words=20):
    top_words = pd.Series(
        ' '.join(df['cleaned_text']).split()
    ).value_counts().head(number_of_words)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    sns.barplot(
        x=top_words.index,
        y=top_words.values,
        palette="viridis"
    )
    plt.xticks(rotation=90)
    plt.title(f"Top 20 most common words in {testament_name}")
    plt.xlabel("Words")
    plt.ylabel("Frequency")
    plt.show()
    return top_words

def plot_top_words_filtered(df, testament_name, stopwords, number_of_words=20):
    words = pd.Series(
        ' '.join(df['cleaned_text']).split()
    )
    filtered_words = words[~words.isin(stopwords)]
    top_words = filtered_words.value_counts().head(number_of_words)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    sns.barplot(
        x=top_words.index,
        y=top_words.values,
        palette="viridis"
    )
    plt.xticks(rotation=90)
    plt.title(f"Top 20 most common words in {testament_name} (filtered)")
    plt.xlabel("Words")
    plt.ylabel("Frequency")
    plt.show()
    return top_words

from wordcloud import WordCloud

def plot_wordcloud(df, testament_name):
    wordcloud = WordCloud(
        width=800,
        height=400,
        background_color='white',
        stopwords=stopwords,
    ).generate(' '.join(df['cleaned_text']))
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    plt.imshow(wordcloud, interpolation='bilinear')
    plt.axis('off')
    plt.title(f"Word Cloud for {testament_name}")
    plt.show()

basic_verses_chapters_books_stats(bible_df, "Bible")
```

# Modeling

```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, accuracy_score

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    bible_df["cleaned_text"],
    bible_df["testament"],
    test_size=0.2,
    stratify=bible_df["testament"],
    random_state=42
)

tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(
    ngram_range=(1,2),
    analyzer="word",
    min_df=3,
    max_features=50000,
    #stop_words=list(stopwords)
)

X_train_tfidf = tfidf.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_tfidf  = tfidf.transform(X_test)

clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=500)
clf.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)

pred = clf.predict(X_test_tfidf)
print("Accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_test, pred))
print(classification_report(y_test, pred))
```

:::{.panel-tabset}
## Plot

```{python}
import numpy as np

feature_names = tfidf.get_feature_names_out()
coef = clf.coef_[0]

top_new = np.argsort(coef)[-20:]
top_old = np.argsort(coef)[:20]

top_features = np.concatenate([top_old, top_new])
top_values = coef[top_features]
top_labels = feature_names[top_features]

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))
positions = np.arange(len(top_features))
plt.barh(positions, top_values)
plt.yticks(positions, top_labels)
plt.title("Top 15 Discriminative Words (Old vs New Testament)")
plt.xlabel("Coefficient Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

labels = clf.classes_

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred, labels=labels)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
cax = ax.imshow(cm, interpolation="nearest")
plt.title("Confusion Matrix")
plt.colorbar(cax)

ax.set_xticks(np.arange(len(labels)))
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(len(labels)))
ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
ax.set_yticklabels(labels)

# Print numbers on matrix
for i in range(len(labels)):
    for j in range(len(labels)):
        ax.text(j, i, cm[i, j], ha="center", va="center")

plt.xlabel("Predicted")
plt.ylabel("Actual")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, auc
from sklearn.preprocessing import label_binarize

# Convert labels to binary (Old = 0, New = 1)
y_bin = label_binarize(y_test, classes=["Old Testament", "New Testament"]).ravel()

idx = list(clf.classes_).index("New Testament")

# Predict probabilities for the New Testament
y_prob = clf.predict_proba(X_test_tfidf)[:, idx]

fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_bin, y_prob)
roc_auc = auc(fpr, tpr)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))
plt.plot(fpr, tpr, linewidth=2, label=f"AUC = {roc_auc:.3f}")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--")
plt.title("ROC Curve")
plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
